theory.intro: A one-to-one function never gives the same output for two different inputs.
facts: A function is one-to-one if every horizontal line meets its graph at most once.
A one-to-one function has an inverse function on its range.
Use the whole stated domain, even when only part of its graph is visible. A polynomial without a domain restriction uses all real inputs.
The vertical line test checks whether a relation is a function; the horizontal line test checks whether a function is one-to-one.
For a quadratic function, use the turning point to restrict the domain to either side, including the turning point.
On either of these restricted domains, the quadratic is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing and has an inverse function.
steps: Use the given domain and apply the horizontal line test.
If a horizontal line meets the graph more than once, the function is not one-to-one.
To restrict a quadratic's domain, find the turning point and choose either side, including the turning point.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The horizontal line $y=1$ meets the graph at $(-2,1)$ and $(0,1)$.
Two different inputs give the same output.
The graph fails the horizontal line test, so the function is not one-to-one.

Each positive horizontal line meets the right branch once; each negative horizontal line meets the left branch once.
The line $y=0$ meets neither branch.
Every horizontal line meets the graph at most once, so the function is one-to-one.

workedExamples.question_text:
Consider $f(x)=(x+2)^2$.
Use the turning point to write down two ways to restrict the domain so that an inverse function exists.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The turning point is $(-2,0)$.
For $x\ge-2$, the graph is strictly increasing and passes the horizontal line test.
For $x\le-2$, the graph is strictly decreasing and passes the horizontal line test.
The two restrictions are $x\ge-2$ and $x\le-2$, each including the turning point.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=-6$ on which $f(x)=x^2+6x+4$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Complete the square to find the turning point.
$f(x)=x^2+6x+9-9+4$
$f(x)=(x+3)^2-5$
The turning point is $(-3,-5)$.
Since $-6<-3$, choose the decreasing branch to the left of the turning point.
Every horizontal line meets this branch at most once.
Including the turning point, the largest such interval is $(-\infty,-3]$.

Every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
$\text{one-to-one}$

A horizontal line above the vertex meets the graph twice.
$\text{not one-to-one}$

foundation.question_text: For $f(x)=(x-5)^2$, use the turning point to write down two ways to restrict the domain so that an inverse function exists.
foundation.solution_text:
The turning point is $(5,0)$.
The graph is strictly decreasing for $x\le5$ and strictly increasing for $x\ge5$.
The two restrictions are $x\le5$ and $x\ge5$.

foundation.question_text: For $f(x)=4-x^2$, use the turning point to write down two ways to restrict the domain so that an inverse function exists.
foundation.solution_text:
The turning point is $(0,4)$.
The graph is strictly increasing for $x\le0$ and strictly decreasing for $x\ge0$.
The two restrictions are $x\le0$ and $x\ge0$.

Every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
$\text{one-to-one}$

development.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=7$ on which $f(x)=(x-3)^2-4$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
development.solution_text:
The turning point is $(3,-4)$.
Since $7>3$, choose the increasing branch.
The largest such interval is $[3,\infty)$.

development.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=-5$ on which $f(x)=(x+1)^2+2$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
development.solution_text:
The turning point is $(-1,2)$.
Since $-5<-1$, choose the decreasing branch.
The largest such interval is $(-\infty,-1]$.

development.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=8$ on which $f(x)=x^2-8x+3$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
development.solution_text:
$f(x)=(x-4)^2-13$
The turning point is $(4,-13)$.
Since $8>4$, choose the increasing branch.
The largest such interval is $[4,\infty)$.

development.question_text: Find the domain on which $f(x)=(x-2)^2-6$ is one-to-one and decreasing, including the turning point.
development.solution_text:
The turning point is $(2,-6)$.
The graph is strictly decreasing to the left of the turning point.
Including the turning point gives $(-\infty,2]$.

A horizontal line above the vertex meets the graph twice.
$\text{not one-to-one}$

development.question_text: Find the domain on which $f(x)=x(x+8)$ is one-to-one and increasing, including the turning point.
development.solution_text:
$f(x)=x^2+8x$
$f(x)=(x+4)^2-16$
The turning point is $(-4,-16)$.
The graph is strictly increasing to the right of the turning point.
Including the turning point gives $[-4,\infty)$.

mastery.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=-2$ on which $f(x)=3x^2+9x-2$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
mastery.solution_text:
$f(x)=3\left(x+\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{35}{4}$
The turning point is $\left(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{35}{4}\right)$.
Since $-2<-\frac{3}{2}$, choose the decreasing branch.
The largest such interval is $\left(-\infty,-\frac{3}{2}\right]$.

mastery.question_text: Find the largest interval containing $x=2$ on which $f(x)=-2x^2+6x+5$ is one-to-one, including the turning point.
mastery.solution_text:
$f(x)=-2\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2+\frac{19}{2}$
The turning point is $\left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{19}{2}\right)$.
Since $2>\frac{3}{2}$, choose the decreasing branch.
The largest such interval is $\left[\frac{3}{2},\infty\right)$.

A horizontal line above the vertex meets the graph twice.
$\text{not one-to-one}$
